rows.selection_reason: With no prior evidence, the most informative first experiment is to establish a simple, well-understood baseline. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest configuration in the search space: a standard PCA-reduced RNA classifier with no image modality, no multiprofile aggregation, and no fusion. This gives a clear performance floor for the RNA signal alone, which is essential before attributing any gains to more complex design choices (image modality, learned encoders, multiprofile aggregation, or fusion strategy). Establishing this baseline first allows subsequent experiments (e.g., image-only, multimodal, alternative encoders) to be interpreted as marginal contributions over a known reference, making the remaining 9 experiments far more informative for isolating which design axes actually matter.

We have only one data point (RNA-only PCA singleprofile at ~48.5% accuracy), so evidence is very sparse. The most critical uncertainty is whether the image modality carries useful signal at all, which determines whether multimodal fusion is worth pursuing in later experiments. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) directly tests this: if image-only accuracy is competitive or better, multimodal configurations become high-priority; if it is poor, we should focus remaining budget on RNA encoder and profile improvements. Using ResNet50 (a standard, well-transferred backbone) keeps the test clean and avoids confounding with an untested ViT encoder. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the modality axis, which is the highest-leverage design decision given the limited 8-experiment budget remaining.

Evidence: RNA-only with PCA n2000 and single profile (config_001) achieves 48.5% accuracy, while image-only ResNet50 (config_010) is weak at 20.8%, indicating RNA is the dominant modality. Uncertainty: We have no data on whether multiprofile aggregation can improve upon the single-profile RNA baseline, and this is the most impactful next design question since it directly extends our best configuration. This experiment (config_002) isolates the effect of switching from single to multiprofile with a simple avgpool aggregation while keeping the same PCA n2000 encoder, cleanly testing whether cell-level aggregation adds value. Choosing avgpool over transformer keeps the experiment minimal and informative: if avgpool shows no gain, it reduces the likelihood that a more complex aggregation will help, saving budget. This is the best use of experiment 3 because it builds directly on our strongest result, tests a single design change (profile + aggregation), and the outcome will strongly inform whether to invest remaining budget in multiprofile variants, alternative RNA encoders, or multimodal fusion.

Evidence: RNA-only multi-profile with PCA n2000 and avgpool (config_002, acc=0.591) is the strongest result so far, showing a ~10.6% gain over single-profile (config_001, acc=0.485). Image-only is very weak (0.208), so the RNA pathway is the clear direction to exploit. Uncertainty: We do not yet know whether a transformer aggregation can capture inter-profile interactions beyond simple averaging, which could push accuracy further. This experiment (config_003) changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding RNA encoder (PCA n2000), profile setting (multiprofile), and modality (RNA-only) constant, giving a clean isolation of the aggregation effect. It is the best next step because it directly exploits the strongest signal found so far, answers a high-value design question with minimal confounding, and will inform whether to invest remaining budget in transformer-based aggregation across other encoders and multimodal settings.

Evidence: RNA-only multi-profile with avgpool (config_002, acc=0.591) is the clear best so far, substantially outperforming single-profile (0.485), transformer aggregation (0.519), and image-only (0.208). This establishes multi-profile + avgpool as the optimal profile/aggregation setting for RNA. Uncertainty: whether a learned RNA encoder (scvi_n200) can capture non-linear structure beyond PCA and push accuracy higher in this best setting. This experiment (config_005: RNA, multi-profile, scvi_n200, avgpool) directly isolates the encoder effect by changing only the RNA encoder from PCA to scvi while holding profile and aggregation at their best-known values, enabling a clean 1:1 comparison with config_002. This is the best use of the 5th experiment because it exploits the strongest direction found, tests the most impactful remaining design choice (representation), and with 5 slots left, establishing the best RNA-only baseline before attempting multimodal fusion is the logical priority given how weak the image signal is (0.208).

Evidence: config_005 (SCVI, multiprofile, avgpool) achieves the best accuracy so far (0.650), and avgpool clearly outperforms transformer for multiprofile aggregation (config_002: 0.591 vs config_003: 0.519 with PCA). SCGPT has not yet been tested in any configuration. Question: Does the SCGPT encoder outperform SCVI under the same favorable settings (multiprofile + avgpool)? This is a clean single-variable comparison isolating the RNA encoder effect. Why this is the best next experiment: With only 4 experiments remaining after this one, establishing the superior RNA encoder is critical before committing budget to multimodal or other architectural extensions. If SCGPT matches or beats SCVI, it opens a new direction; if it underperforms, it confirms SCVI as the best encoder and lets me focus remaining experiments on whether multimodal fusion or other refinements can push past 0.65.

The current best is config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) at 0.650 accuracy. The only aggregation tested with scvi_n200 is avgpool; transformer was only tested with pca_n2000 (where it underperformed avgpool by 0.072). It is possible that the richer, learned scvi_n200 representation interacts differently with transformer aggregation than the linear PCA space does. Config_006 (scvi_n200 + transformer) is a clean single-variable change from the current best, directly isolating the aggregation effect for the top encoder. If transformer wins, we discover a new best; if it confirms avgpool, we lock in the aggregation choice and can spend the remaining 3 experiments exploring multimodal fusion with scvi_n200. This is the highest-information, lowest-risk next step under the tight budget.

Evidence: The best configuration so far is RNA-only with scvi_n200 + multiprofile (0.650–0.653), while image-only with resnet50 is very weak (0.208). We have not yet tested whether a stronger image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) combined with the best RNA setup can improve upon the RNA-only baseline. This experiment (config_038: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) isolates the question of whether adding image features with a powerful pretrained ViT encoder provides complementary signal. Transformer aggregation was marginally preferred for scvi_n200 (0.653 vs 0.650), and concat is the simpler, more standard fusion choice. With only 2 experiments remaining after this one, testing the most promising multimodal combination now is critical: if it beats 0.653, we can fine-tune fusion type in the last experiments; if it does not, we confirm the RNA-only scvi_n200 + multiprofile configuration is optimal and avoid wasting budget on weaker multimodal variants.

The current best is config_038 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat) at 0.721 accuracy. The only untested single-variable perturbation from this best config is the fusion strategy: config_039 swaps concat for weighted fusion while keeping all other settings identical. Evidence from the RNA-only experiments shows transformer aggregation and scvi_n200 are the strongest choices, and the multimodal jump (0.721 vs 0.653 RNA-only) confirms imagenet_vit_l adds substantial value. Testing weighted fusion here directly asks whether a learned or adaptive combination of modalities can outperform simple concatenation, which is the most likely remaining source of improvement. With only 2 experiments left, this is the highest-value exploitation step: if weighted fusion helps, we get a new best; if not, we confirm concat is optimal and the final experiment can focus on any remaining question. No other single change (e.g., swapping to avgpool or resnet50) is as likely to yield a meaningful gain given the existing evidence.

The current best is config_039 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) at 0.725 acc. Evidence strongly supports scvi_n200 as the best RNA encoder, ViT-L as the best image encoder, multiprofile, and weighted fusion. The only remaining uncertainty among the top-tier configurations is the aggregation method in the multimodal setting: transformer (0.725) vs. avgpool. In the RNA-only setting, the gap was negligible (0.653 vs. 0.650), so the multimodal interaction could theoretically shift this. Config_037 (avgpool, weighted) is the single closest untested variant to the current best, changing only aggregation. As the final experiment, it offers the highest (albeit small) probability of exceeding 0.725 while also confirming whether the transformer aggregation's marginal edge in RNA-only carries over to multimodal fusion. All other untested options involve downgrading the RNA encoder (scgpt/PCA) or image encoder (ResNet50), which the evidence strongly indicates would underperform.
